title: Area and constructing motion graphs
learning_outcomes: Use signed area under a velocity-time graph to find displacement.
Distinguish displacement from distance when velocity changes sign.
Construct and translate motion graphs from descriptions and linked graphs.
prior_knowledge_summary: Students can read displacement-time and velocity-time graphs.
Students know that displacement-time gradient gives velocity and velocity-time gradient gives acceleration.
Students can calculate straight and tangent gradients with signs and units.
new_learning: signed area and its connection to displacement
total geometric area and its connection to distance
construction of displacement-time and velocity-time graphs from motion descriptions
knowledge_boundary: Use graph reading, gradient knowledge and elementary geometry only. Do not require constant-acceleration equations or later mechanics.

assessment_demands: combine positive and negative velocity-time graph regions
sketch a graph whose gradient represents changing speed
evidence_basis.canonical_audit: Checked canonical questions, mark schemes and graph figures. 9702_s18_22_q03_b supports signed velocity-time areas; 9702_w20_21_q02_d supports graph construction.

excluded_mapped_parts.9702_m22_22_q02_b: Canonical part is horizontal uniform-motion time, not graph area.
excluded_mapped_parts.9702_m22_22_q02_c: Canonical part is vertical free-fall height, not graph construction.

visual_rules.style: hand-drawn teacher sketch with basic annotations

blocks.title: The graph returns to zero, but the rider did move
body: A cyclist rides forward, turns around and returns to the starting point. The velocity-time graph has one region above the time axis and one below it.
Prediction: if the two regions have equal size, has the cyclist travelled zero distance?
The final displacement can be zero even though the journey has a real length. We need the areas and their signs to separate these two answers.

figure.purpose: Create the opening contradiction between zero displacement and non-zero distance.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn cyclist route out and back beside a velocity-time graph with one equal region above and one below the axis. Do not label the final numerical answers.
figure.alt_text: A cyclist travels out and back while equal velocity-time regions lie above and below the time axis.

blocks.title: Area turns velocity into displacement
blocks.definition: distance in a specified direction from a point
body: For constant velocity, a rectangular region has area velocity multiplied by time.
Its units are (m s^-1) times s, which gives m. That is a displacement unit.
The same idea works for changing velocity by splitting the region into familiar shapes.

figure.purpose: Connect rectangle dimensions, units and displacement.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn velocity-time rectangle labelled velocity and time, with a unit trail m s^-1 times s equals m.
figure.alt_text: A rectangle under a velocity-time graph shows velocity multiplied by time and gives displacement in metres.

blocks.title: The time axis controls the sign
body: Area above the time axis is positive displacement. Area below it is negative displacement.
Add signed areas to find the change of position. Use the magnitude of every area and add those magnitudes to find total distance travelled.
A crossing of the time axis means velocity is zero at that instant. If the sign changes, the direction of motion changes too.

figure.purpose: Compare signed displacement and unsigned distance using the same graph.
figure.brief: Two-column hand-drawn comparison using one velocity-time graph. Left column combines positive and negative signed regions for displacement. Right column adds both region magnitudes for distance.
figure.alt_text: The same two graph regions are subtracted for displacement and added by magnitude for distance.

blocks.title: Walk through an out-and-back journey
body: From 0 to 6.0 s, velocity rises from 0 to +8.0 m s^-1. The positive triangular area is one half times 6.0 times 8.0, so it is +24 m.
From 6.0 to 10.0 s, velocity falls from 0 to -3.0 m s^-1. The region below the axis has magnitude one half times 4.0 times 3.0, so its signed area is -6.0 m.
Displacement = +24 + (-6.0) = +18 m.
Distance = 24 + 6.0 = 30 m. The rider ends 18 m in the positive direction after travelling 30 m in total.

figure.purpose: Model the full signed-area routine with two triangular regions.
figure.brief: Annotated worked velocity-time layout with a positive triangle from 0 to 6 s and a negative triangle from 6 to 10 s. Put separate area calculations beside the regions and a final displacement-versus-distance comparison below.
figure.alt_text: Two triangular velocity-time regions give positive 24 metres and negative 6 metres, leading to 18 metres displacement and 30 metres distance.

blocks.title: Why area below the axis is not negative distance
body: It is natural to think that any region below the axis must make the journey shorter. That idea feels right because its signed value is negative.
The sign records direction, not whether motion happened. Moving back still adds to the length of the path.
So negative area reduces displacement, but its magnitude increases distance.

blocks.title: Build a graph from the motion, one interval at a time
body: First choose a positive direction and write each interval in words.
For a velocity-time graph, constant positive velocity is a horizontal line above the axis. Rest lies on the axis. Constant negative velocity is a horizontal line below it.
A straight sloping velocity-time line means constant acceleration because its gradient is constant.
Mark boundary times first, plot the required velocity at each boundary, then join points using the stated motion.

figure.purpose: Teach graph construction as a sequence of interval decisions.
figure.brief: Three-frame teacher sketch: written motion timeline, boundary points placed on velocity-time axes, then completed piecewise graph. Use positive constant velocity, rest and negative constant velocity.
figure.alt_text: A motion description becomes a timeline, plotted boundary points and then a piecewise velocity-time graph.

blocks.title: Translate velocity-time into displacement-time
body: Use Lesson 4 in reverse: velocity is the gradient of a displacement-time graph.
Positive velocity makes displacement rise. Zero velocity makes displacement horizontal. Negative velocity makes displacement fall.
A larger velocity magnitude needs a steeper displacement-time section.
Keep the displacement-time graph continuous. Position cannot jump instantly just because velocity changes.

figure.purpose: Link velocity sign and magnitude to displacement-time gradient and continuity.
figure.brief: Aligned velocity-time and displacement-time graphs sharing time boundaries. Show positive constant velocity mapping to a rising straight line, zero velocity to a flat line and larger negative velocity magnitude to a steeper falling line.
figure.alt_text: Aligned graphs show how velocity sign and size control the gradient of a continuous displacement-time graph.

blocks.title: A reliable graph routine
items: Identify the axes and choose the positive direction.
Split the motion at every change of behaviour.
For area, calculate each simple shape and attach its sign from its side of the time axis.
For construction, mark times and values before joining points.
Check units, continuity and whether the final story matches the graph.

blocks.title: Resolve the cyclist puzzle
body: Equal regions above and below the axis cancel as signed areas, so the cyclist's displacement is zero.
Both region magnitudes count toward the path length, so the distance is not zero.
A motion graph now tells us more than what happens at each instant. Its gradient, area and shape connect velocity, position and the whole journey.

concepts_taught: Signed area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement.
Total geometric area under a velocity-time graph gives distance travelled.
Velocity sign and magnitude determine displacement-time gradient.
Motion descriptions can be converted into piecewise motion graphs.
misconceptions_addressed: Negative graph area is negative distance.
Zero displacement means no distance was travelled.
A displacement-time graph may jump when velocity changes.
skills_students_can_now_use: Calculate displacement and distance from velocity-time graphs.
Combine rectangular, triangular and trapezoidal regions with correct signs.
Construct velocity-time graphs from interval descriptions.
Translate velocity-time behaviour into a continuous displacement-time graph.
next_lesson_can_assume: Students can read and construct basic motion graphs.
Students can use graph gradients for velocity and acceleration.
Students can use signed velocity-time area for displacement and total area magnitude for distance.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Students know free-fall or projectile-motion models.
